analysis.one_liner: Restricts union organizing and dues, and carves gig and franchise companies out of workplace protections.
analysis.headline: The Employee Rights Act, backed by 39 House Republicans, never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make it harder to form and keep a union. It would require unions to win elections by a majority of all employees in a workplace, not just those who vote; force elections to decertify every union that was recognized without a secret ballot; restrict union dues to bargaining functions; and let employers refuse to bargain in the final 90 days of a contract. It would also state that gig platform workers and franchise employees are not the employer's employees under federal labor and wage law, and let employers prohibit organizing on company-issued devices.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing drives, gig platform companies, and franchisors would gain the most, through higher barriers to union representation and carve-outs from joint-employer and employee-status rules. Individual workers who oppose union representation would gain rights the bill frames as protections: secret-ballot votes on contracts and strikes, written consent before dues fund non-bargaining activity, and limits on how unions use personal information.

how_it_helps.text: It would let an employer refuse to bargain with a union in the final 90 days of a contract if the employer presents evidence that a majority of employees no longer support the union [S2][S3].

It would require union elections to be won by a majority of all employees in the bargaining unit, not just a majority of those voting, meaning low turnout could keep a union out even if most voters wanted one [S3].

It would require the Labor Board to run recertification elections within 120 days for every union voluntarily recognized by an employer, with representation ending if a majority of votes cast reject it [S3].
It would restrict union dues, fees, and assessments to collective bargaining and contract administration unless each employee signs a written, annually expiring authorization [S3].

It would provide that benefits paid by a gig platform company to its workers do not create an employment relationship under federal labor or wage law, and that a franchisor cannot be treated as a joint employer for requiring franchisees to adopt policies on harassment, paid leave, or similar matters [S3].

It would give employers the right to prohibit employees from using company-issued technology to organize, and would state that federal labor law does not protect employees' right to support class or collective lawsuits [S3].

It would require secret-ballot strike votes run by a neutral private organization chosen jointly by the employer and union, with workers voting on the employer's latest contract offer first and the union paying election costs; it would also raise penalties for union misconduct and expand the federal extortion statute to cover union conduct, punishable by up to 20 years [S3].

It would exempt from the National Labor Relations Act any employer majority-owned or controlled by members of a religion that historically objects to unions, and exempt tribal enterprises on tribal lands [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers in unionized or organizing workplaces would bear the cost, through weaker bargaining power, mandatory decertification elections, and dues restrictions. Union members would lose the ability to have their dues fund advocacy beyond bargaining. Gig and franchise workers would remain outside federal protections against misclassification. The bill does include some real protections for individual workers, such as union privacy obligations and notice requirements on authorization cards.

drawbacks.text: The requirement that a union win a majority of all employees in the unit, and the mandated recertification elections for voluntarily recognized unions, would make representation far easier to lose: an election with low turnout could eliminate a union even if most voters wanted it [S3].

The dues restriction would end unions' ability to spend member money on political or policy advocacy without annual written consent from each member, sharply limiting their voice outside the bargaining table [S3].
The gig and franchise provisions would lock in contractor and franchisee status for millions of workers, keeping them outside minimum wage, overtime, and collective bargaining protections [S3].

Narrowing the joint-employer standard to direct, immediate control would make it harder to hold parent companies and staffing arrangements responsible for wages and conditions at the workplaces they influence [S3].

Expanding the federal extortion statute to labor conduct and criminalizing interference with employer technology rights would expose union organizers to prosecution and damages in ways current law does not [S3].

Supporters would have to acknowledge that the bill is framed around individual rights while its central mechanics lower union support thresholds and expand employer discretion during organizing drives [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A few provisions offer genuine individual-worker protections: written dues consent, secret-ballot strike and ratification votes, union privacy duties, and notice requirements on authorization cards are real and would matter to some workers. But these sit inside a bill whose core effect is to make unions much harder to win and keep — through all-employee majorities, forced recertification elections, employer refusal-to-bargain rights, and a criminal-law expansion — and to remove gig and franchise workers from federal protections altogether. The gains flow mostly to employers; the costs fall on workers' collective bargaining power, and the individual-rights provisions do not offset that imbalance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, sat there for over nine months with no hearing or markup, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen (R-GA) introduced the Employee Rights Act on March 24, 2022, and it was referred to the Education and Labor, Judiciary, and Rules committees [S1][S3][S5].
It drew 38 cosponsors, all Republicans, and no Democrats [S4].
Its only action after referral was a November 1, 2022 referral to a Judiciary subcommittee; the committees held no hearings and the House never voted on it [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and the workers who rely on collective bargaining are better off because the bill died, since none of its restrictions on organizing, dues, or recertification took effect. Its business backers gained nothing, but lost nothing either — existing labor law simply remained unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 38 cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrat signed on, and the Democratic House majority took no action on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would raise the bar for winning and keeping a union — all-employee majorities, forced recertification elections, and a right to refuse bargaining in a contract's final 90 days — and add employer rights over company technology and hiring. Those gains come directly at the expense of workers' collective bargaining power.

It would write into federal law that a gig company paying benefits to its workers still has no employment relationship with them, keeping those workers outside minimum wage, overtime, and bargaining protections.

It would bar franchisors from being treated as joint employers of franchise workers for requiring policies on harassment, leave, or child care, shifting responsibility for those workers' conditions onto small franchisees.

The bill would gut union finances by restricting dues to bargaining functions, force recertification elections, and expose organizers to expanded extortion penalties. Unions' ability to bargain collectively is the main vehicle workers have for raising wages and conditions, so their interest in defeating it runs alongside ordinary workers'.

It would exempt tribal businesses from the National Labor Relations Act; workers at those enterprises would lose federal organizing and bargaining rights, though framed as respect for tribal sovereignty.
